llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Survey and unification of probabilistic (non-deterministic) solution concepts for inviscid fluid PDEs—primarily incompressible and compressible (isentropic) Euler equations—motivated by turbulence, ill-posedness and non-uniqueness of weak solutions. The paper (i) systematically presents measure-valued (Young-measure-based) solutions, including dissipative formulations with concentration/defect measures and energy inequalities; (ii) develops and compares several statistical-solution frameworks (trajectory, phase-space/Foiaș–Prodi, Hopf, and moment/correlation-measure-based/Friedmann–Keller); (iii) establishes precise relations/equivalences among statistical notions (notably equivalence between phase-space measures on L2 and correlation measures under support/moment conditions, and projection from trajectory to phase-space); (iv) reviews key analytical properties: global existence for dissipative measure-valued solutions for broad initial data, weak–strong uniqueness/stability via relative energy, and characterization of when measure-valued solutions arise as limits of weak/approximate solutions (incompressible: always; compressible: not always, with necessary Jensen-type A-quasiconvexity constraints and partial sufficiency results).
llm_extracted_info.methodology:
Mathematical analysis and synthesis of existing theory, centered on:
- Young measures and generalized Young measures (oscillation and concentration effects), with weak-* measurability and generation by bounded sequences.
- Definition of dissipative measure-valued solutions for incompressible Euler and isentropic compressible Euler using barycenters, Reynolds-stress/concentration measures m, and dissipation defect D, enforcing PDE only in averaged form plus an energy inequality.
- Construction/existence via vanishing-viscosity limits from Navier–Stokes solutions; passage to limits producing Young measures + defect measures.
- Relative energy/entropy method to prove weak–strong uniqueness and stability (Grönwall estimate) for both incompressible and compressible settings (compressible requires strong solution without vacuum).
- Singular-limit and realizability theory: incompressible case uses convex integration results (Székelyhidi–Wiedemann) showing every mvs is generated by weak solutions; compressible case uses linear relaxation (introducing lifted variables (ρ,m,M,Q)), wave-cone/A-free calculus of variations, A-quasiconvexity and Jensen-type constraints for generability; convex integration + truncation/potential operators yield sufficiency under strong structural assumptions.
- Statistical solutions: defines and compares
  * trajectory measures on solution paths,
  * phase-space time-parametrized measures satisfying Foiaș–Liouville equation tested on cylindrical functionals,
  * Hopf equation via characteristic functionals,
  * moment/correlation-measure hierarchies satisfying an infinite chain of equations.
  Uses measure-theoretic equivalence theorems (correlation measures ↔ measures on Lp), monotone class arguments for measurability, and compactness/approximation arguments to construct solutions.
- Construction methods for statistical solutions (2D Euler focus): (I) compactness of approximating families (e.g., vanishing-viscosity statistical solutions of Navier–Stokes); (II) discrete Krein–Milman approximation on compact sets of trajectories; (III) measurable selection/semi-flow selection plus pushforward of initial measures.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup:
No numerical/empirical experiments are performed (the article is a theoretical survey). Validation is through rigorous mathematical proofs and literature synthesis. The main ‘setups’ are analytical model settings:
- PDEs/benchmarks: incompressible Euler and isentropic compressible Euler; occasional reference to Navier–Stokes for approximation/vanishing-viscosity constructions.
- Domains: bounded domains with impermeability boundary conditions or periodic tori; statistical-solution equivalence and construction are treated mainly on the 2D torus T^2 over a finite time interval [0,T].
- Function spaces/regularity: energy spaces (L2 for velocity; Lγ for density in compressible case), H and H_w for divergence-free L2 fields; H1/vorticity-in-L2 assumptions for constructing 2D statistical solutions; strong solutions in C1 for weak–strong uniqueness.
- Approximation/verification mechanisms: vanishing-viscosity sequences, Young-measure compactness (Banach–Alaoglu), disintegration of defect measures, convex integration realizability results, and equivalence checks via characteristic functionals (Hopf) or correlation hierarchies.
- ‘Benchmarks’ in the survey sense include canonical examples (e.g., vortex sheet generating nontrivial Young limits) and classical theorems (DiPerna–Majda existence, Brenier–De Lellis–Székelyhidi weak–strong uniqueness, Székelyhidi–Wiedemann generation theorem, A-free rigidity counterexamples in compressible case).
llm_extracted_info.limitations:
Key limitations and assumptions emphasized:
- Survey scope: focuses on inviscid models (Euler) and fundamental existence/uniqueness/relations; excludes genuinely stochastic forcing/techniques and excludes long-time/invariant-measure/attractor theory.
- Measure-valued solutions capture only one-point statistics (first/second moments plus defect), not spatial correlations; hence limited for turbulence descriptors requiring multipoint statistics.
- Non-uniqueness persists: mvs are highly non-unique; statistical solutions’ existence/uniqueness can be as hard as deterministic weak solutions, and phase-space ↔ trajectory equivalence is generally open.
- Weak–strong uniqueness for compressible Euler requires strong solution with strictly positive density (no vacuum), with only partial extensions.
- Realizability by weak solutions differs by model: incompressible mvs are always generable by weak solutions, hence may not provide additional selection; compressible mvs are not always generable, but available sufficient conditions are restrictive (e.g., dimension d≥2, specific γ=1+2/d for sufficiency theorem, lower density bound ρ≥η, continuity constraints on energy, and additional barycenter/potential-structure assumptions).
- Equivalence between phase-space and correlation-measure statistical solutions in the paper is proved under bounded-support/compactness-type assumptions; relaxing these assumptions is technically difficult.
- Correlation measures require diagonal continuity, which may exclude limits of oscillatory sequences (too strong for some singular limits), limiting applicability as a generalized limit object.
- Construction of statistical solutions often relies on compactness of deterministic solutions/approximations (e.g., 2D with H1/vorticity controls); for general initial data where only convex-integration solutions exist, lack of compactness obstructs current methods.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions:
Open directions highlighted or naturally suggested:
- Develop existence theory for statistical solutions more directly from the Foiaș–Liouville (or Hopf) equations, potentially independent of deterministic compactness/existence results, and applicable where deterministic weak existence is unknown.
- Clarify the converse of Theorem 10: characterize when a phase-space statistical solution arises as the time-marginals of a trajectory statistical solution; find either a general proof or counterexamples.
- Better understand the map from correlation measures to first-marginal Young measures: whether every finite-energy Young measure can be extended to a full correlation measure (surjectivity) and whether such extension is unique (injectivity).
- Enrich measure-valued frameworks to incorporate correlations (multi-point statistics) while remaining stable under oscillatory limits; reconcile diagonal-continuity constraints with turbulent/oscillatory regimes.
- Improve realizability/selection criteria in the compressible case: close the gap between necessary Jensen/A-quasiconvex constraints and sufficient conditions; relax restrictive assumptions (energy continuity, lower density bounds, special γ, and L∞/Calderón–Zygmund-related technical hurdles).
- Strengthen weak–strong uniqueness/stability results for statistical solutions (especially phase-space formulations), including vacuum-tolerant compressible theory.
- Produce explicit nontrivial examples of statistical solutions beyond convex combinations of Dirac masses; develop constructive/numerical approximation frameworks consistent with correlation-measure or phase-space notions.

research_study_list.full_text: arXiv:2307.05436v1  [math.DG]  11 Jul 2023 CONFORMAL ACTIONS OF SOL V ABLE LIE GROUPS ON CLOSED LORENTZIAN MANIFOLDS VINCENT PECAST AING Abstract. We consider conformal actions of solvable Lie groups on clos ed Lorentzian manifolds. With [ Pec18], in which we addressed similar questions for semi-simple L ie groups, this work contributes to the understanding of the id entity component G of the conformal group of compact Lorentzian manifolds. In the ﬁrs t part of the article, we prove that G is inessential if and only if its nilradical is inessential. In the second, we assume the nilradical essential and establish conformal ﬂatness of the metric on an open subset, under certain algebraic hypothesis on the so lvable radical. This is related to the Lorentzian Lichnerowicz conjecture. Finall y, we consider the remaining situations where our methods do not apply to prove conformal ﬂatness, and conclude that for an essential compact Lorentzian n-manifold, n ⩾ 3, the radical of its conformal group admits a local embedding into O(2, n). Contents 1. Introduction 1 2. Embedding theorem and other anterior results 8 3. Inessential actions 9 4. Essential actions 17 5. Proof of Theorem 1: embedding of the radical into so(2,n) 32 References 35 1. Introduction This work has two main motivations. First, we would like to ob tain a classiﬁcation, up to local isomorphism, of conformal groups of compact Lore ntzian manifolds, that would generalize that of Adams-Stuck-Zeghib, in which the i dentity component of their isometry groups are classiﬁed. Secondly , the Lorentzian version of a conjecture of Lich- nerowicz asserts that essential closed Lorentzian manifol ds are conformally ﬂat. W e aim to establish conformal ﬂatness of these manifolds, assumin g that their conformal group satisﬁes extra algebraic assumption. Let us ﬁrst recall bri eﬂy these problems. Date: July 12, 2023. This work has been supported by the F rench government, throu gh the UCA JEDI Investments in the F uture project managed by the National Research Agency (ANR ) with the reference number ANR-15- IDEX-01. 1CONFORMAL ACTIONS OF SOL V ABLE LIE GROUPS ON CLOSED LORENTZIAN MANIFOLDS 2 1.1. General context. A conformal diﬀeomorphism of a pseudo-Riemannian manifold (M,g) is an element f ∈ Diﬀ( M) for which there exists ϕ ∈ C ∞(M), ϕ > 0, such that f∗g= ϕg. W e denote by [g] the conformal class of g and we call (M,[g]) a pseudo- Riemannian conformal structure. W e also denote by Conf(M,[g]) the group of conformal diﬀeomorphisms of (M,[g]). A natural question is to know if a conformal structure (M,[g]) admits conformal transformations which are not isometries of any metric g′ in the conformal class. Deﬁnition 1.1. Let (M,[g]) be a pseudo-Riemannian conformal structure. A sub- group H < Conf(M,[g]) is said to be inessential if there exists g′ ∈ [g] such that H <Isom(M,g′). Otherwise, it is said to be essential. If Conf(M,[g]) is essential, we say that (M,[g]) is essential. F or positive-deﬁnite metrics, a closed subgroup H of conformal transformations is essential if and only if it acts non-properly on M. So, for M compact, this is equivalent to the non-compactness of the conformal group. These proper ties are no longer true for higher signatures, so one of the ﬁrst questions is how to char acterize essentiality . In dimension at least 3, a conformal class of pseudo-Riemannian metrics deﬁnes a rigid geometric structure , be it in Gromov’s sense [ Gro88], or in the sense that it is equivalent to a normalized Cartan geometry modeled on Einp,q , the pseudo-Riemannian analogue of the Möbius sphere. As a consequence, Conf(M,[g]) has the structure of a Lie trans- formation group (possibly non connected) and a natural prob lem is to determine which Lie groups arise in this way , and on which geometry they can ac t. W e will concentrate here on conformal structures on compact manifolds and to the identity component of their conformal group. Lichnerowicz conjectured in the 1960’s that if a closed Riem annian manifold is essen- tial, then it is conformally equivalent to the round sphere. More generally , a “V ague general conjecture” of D’Ambra and Gromov ([ DG91], §0.8) asserts that rigid geometric structures with large automorphism groups can be classiﬁed , as it had been the case when F errand and Obata proved Lichnerowicz’s conjecture, ﬁ rst as formulated above, and then its non-compact analogue [ F er71, F er96, Oba71], see also [ Sch95] and the ex- tension to the CR case. Since then, various people have been w orking on generalizations to other geometric structures, notably on a projective vers ion of Lichnerowicz’s conjec- ture ( e.g. [Mat07]). It appeared that a pseudo-Riemannian analogue of F erran d-Obata’s theorem is not plausible [ F ra05]. One of the reasons is that it is deeply related to the “rank 1 nature” of conformal Riemannian structures ([ F ra07]), whereas other signatures are modeled on higher-rank parabolic geometries . In [ DG91], the authors asked if gen- eral compact pseudo-Riemannian manifolds admitting an ess ential conformal group are conformally ﬂat, i.e. locally conformally equivalent to the ﬂat pseudo-Euclidea n space Rp,q . F rances gave counter-examples to this question in all sign atures of metric index at least 2 ([F ra15]). The case of Lorentzian metrics remains however open, and led to the following problem. Conjecture 1. Let (M,[g]) be a compact, conformal Lorentzian structure. If it is essen - tial, then it is conformally ﬂat.CONFORMAL ACTIONS OF SOL V ABLE LIE GROUPS ON CLOSED LORENTZIAN MANIFOLDS 3 Recently , a proof for 3-dimensional, real-analytic, compa ct Lorentzian manifolds has been established in [ FM21], and the main result of [ MP22] implies that it is also true for compact, real-analytic Lorentzian manifolds with ﬁnite fu ndamental group. Apart from these general results, various works have been de aling with compact pseudo-Riemannian manifolds with “large” conformal group s. It appeared that if a semi-simple Lie group S of non-compact type acts conformally on a closed pseudo- Riemannian manifold of signature (p,q), then RkR(S) ⩽ min(p,q) + 1 [Zim87] and if equality holds, then the manifold is a quotient of the univer sal cover of Einp,q by a cyclic group [ BN02, FZ05]. In [ Pec19], the opposite situation of actions by rank 1 sim- ple Lie groups is considered and similar conclusions are obt ained when the metric index is minimal. F or the Lorentzian signature, it is proved in [ Pec18] that if a non-compact semi-simple Lie groups acts conformally essentially on a cl osed Lorentzian manifold, then it is conformally ﬂat (see § 1.3 below). In another direction, it is natural to consider the “solvabl e part” of the conformal group of these manifolds and to derive geometric or dynamica l information. F rances and Melnick proved in [ FM10] that if a nilpotent Lie group N, with nilpotence degree k, acts conformally on a closed pseudo-Riemannian manifold o f signature (p,q), then k ⩽ 2 min(p,q) + 1 and that if equality holds, the manifold is again a quotient o f the universal cover of Einp,q by a cyclic group. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Studies conformal actions of connected solvable Lie groups on closed (compact, without boundary) Lorentzian manifolds (dimension n≥3) to advance classification of identity components of conformal groups and the Lorentzian Lichnerowicz conjecture (essential ⇒ conformally flat). Main results: (1) Embedding obstruction (Theorem 1): any essential connected solvable subgroup R<Conf(M,[g]) has Lie algebra r embedding into so(2,n), matching the conformally flat model Ein_{1,n−1}. (2) Essentiality reduction (Theorem 2): for solvable R with nilradical N, if N is inessential then R is inessential; for non-abelian N, essentiality is characterized by the last nonzero term N_k of the lower central series. (3) Nilpotent actions (Theorem 3): for connected nilpotent H acting locally faithfully conformally on closed Lorentzian (M,g), derive strong structural/dynamical constraints: abelian H acts locally freely on an open-dense set (dim H≤n); if H is non-abelian and essential then an open subset is conformally flat; moreover nilpotence degree ≤3 and the last central term is 1-dimensional with order-2 singularities. (4) Under broad algebraic hypotheses on the solvable radical (failure of certain “purely imaginary weight” configurations), essentiality forces existence of unipotent/nonlinear holonomy singularities, implying conformal flatness on a nonempty open set. (5) Remaining non-flat cases are reduced to an explicit algebraic form (Proposition 1.9): r≅a⋉_ρ n with n abelian, a abelian, ρ faithful semisimple, and real parts of complex weights lying in {0,λ}; in these cases an explicit embedding into so(2,n) is constructed, proving Theorem 1.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Uses tools from conformal Lorentzian geometry as normalized Cartan geometries modeled on the Einstein universe Ein_{1,n−1}=G/P with G=PO(2,n). Key techniques: Zimmer/Bader–Frances–Melnick embedding theorem for Cartan geometries to relate dynamics of amenable subgroups (e.g., 1-parameter subgroups) preserving measures to algebraic subgroups of Ad(P), yielding conformal/isometric representations on tangent quotients along orbits. Employs analysis of holonomy of conformal maps/vector fields at fixed points via Cartan connection; studies unipotent holonomy and local linearization criteria (Frances) and uses Frances–Melnick normal forms results: existence of non-linear unipotent holonomy or order-2 singularities forces conformal flatness on an open set. Combines Lie algebra structure theory of solvable/nilpotent groups (nilradical, lower central series, weights of the adjoint action) with Lorentzian causal constraints on orbits (isotropic/lightlike, degenerate planes), plus renormalization/coboundary arguments using invariant functions like g(X,X) to upgrade conformal invariance to isometric invariance (inessentiality). Final step: explicit matrix embeddings of the remaining solvable Lie algebras into so(2,n) using restricted root-space decomposition and weight data.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: No computational/empirical experiments. Validation is purely mathematical: theorems proved via rigorous arguments, leveraging prior results (BFM09 embedding theorem; FM10/FM13 on nilpotent actions and normal forms; Pec18 for semisimple actions; linearization criteria). ‘Benchmarks’ are canonical geometric models (Einstein universe Ein_{1,n−1}, Minkowski patches, and the conformal group PO(2,n)) and known classification results for isometry groups (Adams–Stuck–Zeghib) used as context/comparison. Conformal flatness conclusions are established by showing existence of suitable singularities/holonomy and invoking known rigidity theorems rather than by dataset evaluation.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Results are specific to Lorentzian signature and compact manifolds (n≥3); many arguments exploit Lorentzian causal structure (lightlike directions) and may not extend to higher index where counterexamples exist. Conformal flatness is obtained only on a nonempty open subset in general (global conformal flatness may require extra assumptions such as real-analyticity to extend from open set). Some statements require local faithfulness or faithfulness (e.g., abelian H≅R^{n−1} case in Theorem 3(1)(c)/Proposition 4.17). The classification is not complete: while Theorem 1 gives an algebraic embedding obstruction, the paper does not fully classify which solvable subgroups of O(2,n) occur as radicals of conformal groups of closed Lorentzian manifolds; remaining cases are reduced to an explicit algebraic family (Prop. 1.9) but geometric realization/classification is left open. Methods relying on Zimmer’s theorem require invariant measures/amenability arguments and may not apply to certain non-amenable or more general settings; some edge cases (e.g., presence of non-compact Levi factor) behave differently (Hopf manifold example).
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: (1) Realization/classification problem: determine which solvable Lie subgroups of O(2,n) can occur as the solvable radical of Conf(M,[g])0 for closed Lorentzian n-manifolds; aim for an Adams–Stuck–Zeghib–type classification in the conformal category. (2) Strengthen toward Lorentzian Lichnerowicz conjecture: remove extra algebraic hypotheses and upgrade ‘open subset conformally flat’ to global conformal flatness in smooth (non-analytic) category; understand analytic continuation mechanisms beyond real-analyticity. (3) Study essential flows: decide whether any essential conformal action on a closed Lorentzian manifold must contain an essential 1-parameter subgroup (conformal vector field) and analyze its dynamics/holonomy. (4) Extend techniques to broader signatures or non-compact manifolds where partial results still hold (e.g., abelian actions locally free on open-dense sets) and clarify which parts fail in higher index. (5) Construct and classify examples realizing the ‘remaining algebraic configurations’ (Prop. 1.9) and analyze their geometry (orbit structure, holonomy, global topology), possibly via quotients of Ein_{1,n−1} or other Cartan-geometric constructions.

research_study_list.full_text: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 189, 2022 ACML 2022 RoLNiP: Robust Learning Using Noisy Pairwise Comparisons Samartha S Maheshwara samartha.s@students.iiit.ac.in and Naresh Manwani naresh.manwani@iiit.ac.in Machine Learning Lab, Kohli Research Block, IIIT Hyderabad, India Editors: Emtiyaz Khan and Mehmet Gönen Abstract This paper presents a robust approach for learning from noisy pairwise comparisons. We propose suﬃcient conditions on the loss function under which the risk minimization frame- work becomes robust to noise in the pairwise similar dissimilar data. Our approach does not require the knowledge of noise rate in the uniform noise case. In the case of conditional noise, the proposed method depends on the noise rates. For such cases, we oﬀer a provably correct approach for estimating the noise rates. Thus, we propose an end-to-end approach to learning robust classiﬁers in this setting. We experimentally show that the proposed approach RoLNiP outperforms the robust state-of-the-art methods for learning with noisy pairwise comparisons. Keywords: Pairwise comparisons, label noise, robust learning, noise rate estimation 1. Introduction Standard classiﬁer learning requires pointwise labeled data. However, in many applications, getting pointwise labeled data is not possible. In many applications, the data comes in the pairwise comparison of two examples. For example, whether two samples belong to the same category or not. A frequent use case of this setting is a large-scale annotation framework, e.g., crowd clustering (Gomes et al., 2011; Yi et al., 2012). Bao et al. (2018) propose an approach that can learn from similar and unlabeled data points. Shimada et al. (2021) propose an empirical risk minimization framework to learn from pairwise similarity data. However, their approach is limited to linear methods. (Hsu et al., 2019) propose a probabilistic framework for learning from pairwise similar, dissimilar data and extend it for deep learning settings. In practical situations, the pairwise annotations received suﬀer from noise due to subjective or objective issues. Thus, two examples may belong to the same class and are annotated to be diﬀerent and vice-versa. Figure 1 shows a toy setting of pairwise similar dissimilar data and its noisy version. To deal with this situation, we need robust models for such noisy pairwise comparisons. We quickly review how noisy label setting is dealt with in standard classiﬁcation problems and borrow some ideas to build robust models for pairwise data. Label noise in the standard classiﬁcation problem has been well addressed. Manwani and Sastry (2013) characterized robustness under label noise and shown that convex losses do not lead to robust risk minimization. For binary classiﬁcation, Ghosh et al. (2015) show that if a loss function satisﬁes the conditionl(f(.),1) + l(f(.),−1) = K for some ﬁniteK, then © 2022 S.S. Maheshwara & N. Manwani. arXiv:2303.02341v1  [cs.LG]  4 Mar 2023Maheshwara Manwani Figure 1: Pairwise Similarity/Dissimilarity Data. The similarity label is +1 when the examples in the pair belong to the same class, then and -1 otherwise. The last column shows the corrupted similarity labels. risk minimization becomes robust to label noise under that loss. Loss functions like ramp loss, sigmoid loss, and probit loss are robust against label noise as they satisfy the property mentioned above (Ghosh et al., 2015). On the other hand, Natarajan et al. (2013) proposes a loss correction-based approach to learning with noisy labels. In this approach, given a loss function, a new loss function is derived such that risk minimization under the new loss is robust to label noise. This approach (Natarajan et al., 2013) requires noise rate as an input. Patrini et al. (2017) proposed a data-dependent approach that can eﬃciently estimate the noise rates. There is not much work in learning binary classiﬁers using noisy pairwise similar-dissimilar data. The existing approach in this setting Dan et al. (2021) extends the loss correction based approach proposed in (Natarajan et al., 2013). However, the applicability of their approach (Dan et al., 2021) is limited for the following reasons. (a) Their approach requires noise rate as an input for diﬀerent cases of SD label noise. (b) They do not provide a provably correct way to estimate the noise rates. (c) Their experimental results are limited to squared error loss only. This paper proposes a new approach for learning robust classiﬁers using noisy pairwise similar dissimilar data. The proposed approach does not change the loss function at all. Instead, it is based on the principle of robust loss functions. We propose the conditions under which risk minimization becomes robust to the SD label noise pairwise similar dissimilar data. We use the acronymRoLNiP (Robust Learning usingNoisy Pairwise comparisons) for our approach. We make the following contributions to this work.RoLNiP Our Contributions: 1. We derive suﬃciency conditions under which the risk minimization framework becomes robust to SD label noise in similar dissimilar data. • Uniform SD Label Noise:In this case, if the loss function satisﬁes the condition l(f(.),1) + l(f(.),−1) = K,∀f ∈F for some ﬁniteK, then we show that the risk minimization becomes robust as long as the uniform noise rate is less than 0.5. RoLNiP does not require noise rate as an input for the uniform noise case. In contrast, the loss correction-based approach (Shimada et al., 2021) requires the noise rate to learn a robust classiﬁer. • SD Conditional SD Label Noise: In this case, if the loss function satisﬁes the conditionl(f(.),1) + l(f(.),−1) = K,∀f ∈F for some ﬁniteK, then we can scale the loss function(l(.,.) such that the scaled loss function becomes robust to the label noise. Experiments In this section, we present experimental results to illustrate the robustness of the proposed approach in the presence of noisy pairwise similarity dis-similarity data. We compare performances of risk minimization with sigmoid loss, ramp loss, mean absolute error (MAE) loss, and mean squared error (MSE) loss with Deep Neural Network (DNN) model architecture. We show experimental results on ﬁve real-world binary classiﬁcation datasets from the UCI ML repository (Dua and Graﬀ, 2017). These datasets are Adult, Breast Cancer, Ionosphere, Phishing, and W8a. To show that the proposed approach works eﬃciently for large-scale image datasets, we show experiments with the CIFAR-10 dataset (Krizhevsky et al.). In the CIFAR-10 dataset, we considered two classes (airplane vs. automobile) for the experiments. 6.1. Creating Noise-free and Noisy Pairwise Similarity Dissimilarity Datasets We randomly choose pair of examples from the original dataset to obtain pairwise data and assign the SD label based on whether they belong to the same class. We call this noise-free pairwise data SSD. We induce SD label noise into the pairwise data discussed above to obtain noisy datasets. We ﬂip the SD label based on the noise rate for every pair of examples in the setSSD. This noisy data is denoted asSη SD. We vary the noise rate (η) for uniform noise cases from 10% to 40%. And for SD conditional SD noise, we provide results on 4 combinations ofηS and ηD. These combinations are (15%,20%), (20%,10%), (20%,25%) and (30%,25%). 6.2. Experimental Setup for The Proposed Approach We train a neural network with three hidden layers for each dataset and noise rate using pairwise similar, dissimilar data. For the CIFAR-10 dataset, we use transfer learning to learn the classiﬁer by adding the layers mentioned above to the pre-trained VGG-19 model. The best architecture of the classiﬁer we used for experiments is a three-layer deep neural network with rectiﬁed linear unit (ReLU) activation function between any two consecutive layers. The number of nodes in the ﬁrst, second, and third hidden layers is 128, 32, and 8, respectively. The output layer uses the sigmoid activation function. We trained with a mini-batch of size 256. We used simple gradient descent with decreasing step size and a momentum term (Adam optimizer). We used PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) library for deep learning. For Adam optimizer, we used the default values (learning rate =0.001,β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999,ϵ = 10−8, weight decay=0). We train neural networks with diﬀerent loss functions (sigmoid, ramp, and absolute error loss). The risk function is a modiﬁcation of the binary classiﬁcation risk function that accommodates the pairwise classiﬁcation problem. We used a 10-fold cross-validation approach to generate all the results. The results reported are averaged over ten such independent runs. We report results for each setting with standard deviation.RoLNiP 6.3. Experiments with Noise Rate Estimation As discussed earlier, noise rate estimation is required for SD conditional SD label noise. For the noise rate estimation classiﬁer, we use one hidden layer (with eight nodes) neural network with a dropout layer between the hidden layer and output layer. We used rectiﬁed linear unit (ReLU) activation function in the hidden layer. We used the cross-entropy loss function with the Adam optimizer. We randomly used 80% for training and 20% for testing sets. The training set is corrupted with the required amount of class conditional label noise before being fed into the classiﬁer for training. We obtain the estimated noise rates using the test set from the learnt classiﬁer. We report estimated noise rates for each dataset obtained by averaging over ten independent runs. Noise rate estimation results are reported in Table 1 for various datasets and noise rates. We observe that the noise rates estimated by the proposed noise rate estimation approach are very close to the actual noise rates. We make the following observations from the results. • RoLNiP Versus LCNiP: We observe that with actual as well as estimated noise rates, RoLNiP outperforms LCNiP for Adult, Breast Cancer, Phishing, and W8a datasets for all combinations of noise rates. For the Ionosphere dataset, RoLNiP outperforms LCNiP for all noise combinations except the (20%,10%) case. For the (20%,10%) case, the performance of RoLNiP is comparable to LCNiP. For the CIFAR-10 dataset, RolNiP and LCNiP perform comparably to each other except for the (30%,25%) noise case. • RoLNiP with Sigmoid Loss, Ramp Loss and Absolute Error Loss: We observe that sigmoid loss, ramp loss and absolute error loss show robust behavior with SD conditional SD label noise. Thus, overall, the proposed approach RoLNiP outperforms the state-of-the-art LCNiP (Dan et al., 2021) on diﬀerent datasets and various noise rates. 7. We show that the proposed method is robust to uniform and conditional noise cases. The proposed approach does not require the noise rate to be known for uniform noise; however, the conditional noise case needs noise rate as input. We oﬀer a provably correct approach for learning noise rates to deal with this situation. We experimentally show that the proposed method performs better than the state-of-the-art approaches in various noise settings and with multiple datasets. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Addresses learning a binary classifier when supervision is only noisy pairwise similarity/dissimilarity (SD) labels (whether two examples share the same class). Proposes RoLNiP, a robust empirical risk minimization framework that (i) gives sufficient loss-function conditions for noise-tolerant SD risk minimization under uniform SD label noise without needing the noise rate (η<0.5), (ii) extends to SD-conditional noise with a provably derived loss scaling requiring ηS, ηD and ηS+ηD<1, and (iii) provides a provably correct, end-to-end noise-rate estimation method for the conditional-noise case. Empirically demonstrates improved robustness over a loss-correction baseline (LCNiP/Dan et al., 2021) across tabular datasets and a CIFAR-10 binary subset.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Builds on a pairwise SD risk decomposition (Shimada et al., 2021) where standard classification risk is rewritten using expectations over similar pairs pS(x,x') and dissimilar pairs pD(x,x'). Defines an adjusted per-example loss L(z,t) from a base loss l(z,y) using class priors (π+, π−). Key robustness condition: symmetry/constant-sum property l(f(x),1)+l(f(x),−1)=K (finite constant), satisfied by non-convex/symmetric losses (0–1, ramp, sigmoid, probit; also discussed MAE variant). Uniform SD noise: shows noisy risk equals ηK + (1−2η)RSD(f), so minimizer is unchanged for η<0.5. SD-conditional noise: derives a modified loss \hat{L} that keeps positive-pair term unchanged and scales negative-pair term by a constant C (function of πS, πD, ηS, ηD), proving the minimizer matches the clean-risk minimizer when ηS+ηD<1. Noise-rate estimation: adapts “anchor/perfect example” idea (Patrini et al., 2017) to pairwise setting by training a network h on concatenated pair features [x1;x2] to estimate p(\tilde{τ}=1|x1,x2); selects most-confident predicted-similar and predicted-dissimilar pairs from a held-out set to estimate \hat{ηS}=p(\tilde{τ}=-1|\bar{x}S1,\bar{x}S2) and \hat{ηD}=p(\tilde{τ}=1|\bar{x}D1,\bar{x}D2).
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Datasets: five UCI binary datasets (Adult, Breast Cancer, Ionosphere, Phishing, W8a) plus CIFAR-10 restricted to two classes (airplane vs automobile). Pairwise data generation: randomly sample pairs from original pointwise-labeled data to create noise-free SD dataset SSD with τ=+1 if same class else −1; inject SD label noise by flipping τ to obtain S^η_SD. Noise settings: uniform η in {0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}; SD-conditional combinations (ηS,ηD) in {(0.15,0.20),(0.20,0.10),(0.20,0.25),(0.30,0.25)}. Models: for UCI datasets, a DNN classifier with 3 hidden layers (128,32,8) with ReLU, sigmoid output; trained with Adam (lr 1e−3, default betas), batch size 256. For CIFAR-10, transfer learning with pretrained VGG-19 plus the same added layers. Losses evaluated: sigmoid loss, ramp loss, absolute error (MAE-like) in RoLNiP; baseline LCNiP uses squared error with loss correction and requires noise rates (actual for uniform; estimated for conditional). Validation: 10-fold cross-validation; results averaged over 10 independent runs with standard deviation. Noise-rate estimation experiment: separate small network (1 hidden layer of 8 units + dropout, ReLU) trained with cross-entropy on concatenated pair features using 80/20 train/test split; estimated noise rates reported and shown close to true rates.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Relies on sufficient (not necessary) symmetry condition l(f,1)+l(f,−1)=K, which excludes common convex losses (hinge, log, squared error) and may require non-convex optimization (e.g., ramp) with potential local minima/optimization instability; theoretical guarantees are for risk minimizers, not necessarily for practical SGD-trained deep nets. Conditional-noise robustness requires knowing/estimating ηS, ηD and assumes ηS+ηD<1; performance depends on noise-rate estimation quality. Noise-rate estimation assumes existence of “perfect/anchor” pairs with p(τ=1|x)=1 and p(τ=−1|x)=1, which may not hold in complex/high-dimensional or overlapping-class settings; selecting most-confident pairs may be brittle under severe noise or model miscalibration. Framework and experiments focus on binary classification; multiclass extension is not developed. Pair construction procedure is random and may not reflect realistic pair sampling biases; computational cost scales with number of pairs and may be large for big datasets if many pairs are used.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Extend RoLNiP theory and algorithms to multiclass classification and structured similarity relations (beyond binary same/different). Develop robustness results for broader loss families (e.g., approximate symmetry, bounded losses, calibrated surrogates) and study optimization/consistency with deep networks. Improve conditional-noise handling without explicit noise-rate estimation (or with joint end-to-end estimation) and relax the “perfect pair” assumption using techniques like confident learning, EM-style latent variable models, or calibration-aware estimation. Study non-uniform instance-dependent pairwise noise (noise depends on x1,x2), adversarial/annotator-specific noise, and biased pair sampling typical in crowdsourcing. Evaluate on larger-scale and more diverse benchmarks (face verification, metric learning, graph-based similarity data) and analyze pair budget/sample complexity, computational trade-offs, and theoretical generalization bounds under pairwise supervision.

research_study_list.full_text: arXiv:2405.12260v1  [math.ST]  20 May 2024 On an upper bound of the set of copulas with a given curvilinear section Yao Ouyanga ∗ Yonghui Suna Hua-Peng Zhangb† a Faculty of Science, Huzhou University, Huzhou, Zhejiang 313000, China b School of Science, Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Nanjing 210023, China Abstract The characterizations when two natural upper bounds of the set of copulas with a given diagonal section are copulas have been well studied in the literature. Given a curvilinear section, however, there is only a partial result concerning the characterization when a natural upper bound of the set of copulas is a copula. In this paper, we completelysolve the characterization problem for this natural upper bound to bea copula in the curvilinear case. Keywords Copula; Diagonal section; Curvilinear section. 1 Introduction (Bivariate) copulas, as functions joining bivariate distribution func tions to their one-dimensional marginal distribution functions according to Sklar ’s theorem [10], are indispensable for tackling the issues of non-normality and non-lin earity in modern ﬁnance [1]. In view of the fact that the tail dependence of t wo ran- dom variables is determined by the diagonal and/or opposite diagona l sections of the underlying copula, there have been several works devoted to studying copulas with given diagonal and/or opposite diagonal sections (see , for in- stance, [2, 4, 5, 9]). Given a diagonal section, while the smallest copu la exists, the greatest one may not. This motivates the interest of charact erizing when ∗ Email:oyy@zjhu.edu.cn † Corresponding author. Email:huapengzhang@163.com 1two natural upper bounds of the set of copulas with a given diagona l section are copulas (see [6, 8, 9, 11]). By bending the diagonal into a curve, De Baets et al. [3] investigate d the degree of asymmetry of a (quasi-)copula with respect to a curve. In particular, they obtained the smallest copula with a given curvilinear section. Zou et al. [12] continued to present the greatest quasi-copula with a given curvilin ear section. Under some additional assumptions, they characterized when the greatest quasi- copula with a given curvilinear section is a copula. The aim of this paper is to completely solve the characterization when the greatest quasi- copula with a given curvilinear section is a copula without any additional assumption . The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We recall some ba sic notions and results related to (quasi-)copulas as well as that with a given curvi- linear section in Section 2. Section 3 is devoted to the characterizat ion theorem. We end with future work in Section 4. 2 Preliminaries In this section, we recall some basic notions and results related to ( quasi-)copulas as well as that with a given curvilinear section. Deﬁnition 2.1. [7] A (bivariate) copula is a function C : [0 , 1]2 → [0, 1] satis- fying: (C1) the boundary condition, i.e., C(u, 0) = C(0, u ) = 0 and C(u, 1) = C(1, u ) = u (∀ u ∈ [0, 1]); (C2) the 2-increasing property, i.e., V (R) ≥ 0 for any rectangle R = [ u1, u 2] × [v1, v 2], where V (R) = C(u2, v 2) − C(u2, v 1) − C(u1, v 2) + C(u1, v 1). Deﬁnition 2.2. [7] A (bivariate) quasi-copula is a function Q : [0 , 1]2 → [0, 1] satisfying (C1) and the following conditions: (Q1) Q is increasing in each variable; (Q2) Q is Lipschitz, i.e., for all u1, u 2, v 1, v 2 ∈ [0, 1], it holds that |Q(u1, v 1) − Q(u2, v 2)| ≤ | u1 − u2| + |v1 − v2|. 2Note that (C1) and (C2) together imply both (Q1) and (Q2), i.e., every copula is a quasi-copula, but not vice versa. Three important copula s are W, M and Π given by W (u, v ) = max {u + v − 1, 0}, M (u, v ) = min {u, v } and Π( u, v ) = uv. [8] A diagonal function is a function δ : [0 , 1] → [0, 1] with the properties: (D1) δ(1) = 1 and δ(t) ≤ t for all t ∈ [0, 1]; (D2) 0 ≤ δ(t2) − δ(t1) ≤ 2(t2 − t1) for all t1, t 2 ∈ [0, 1] with t1 ≤ t2. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Provides a complete necessary-and-sufficient characterization of when the natural greatest quasi-copula A_{\Gamma_\varphi} associated with a prescribed curvilinear section \Gamma_\varphi (along v=\varphi(u)) is actually a copula (i.e., 2-increasing). This resolves an open gap left by prior work that only gave partial results under extra assumptions. The characterization shows that A_{\Gamma_\varphi} is a copula iff either \Gamma_\varphi equals m_\varphi(t)=\min\{t,\varphi(t)\} everywhere (yielding the Fréchet upper bound M), or the set where \Gamma_\varphi<m_\varphi decomposes into pairwise disjoint countably many open intervals on which \Gamma_\varphi must have a specific two-piece form, together with a global 'compatibility' condition coupling these intervals through \varphi.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Purely theoretical analysis in copula/quasi-copula theory. The paper studies the explicit extremal construction A_{\Gamma_\varphi}(u,v)=\min\{\cdot\} involving maxima of deviations (t-\Gamma_\varphi(t)) and (\varphi(t)-\Gamma_\varphi(t)) over intervals (Eq. (2)), and derives 2-increasingness by analyzing the signed volume V(R) over rectangles. Key steps: (1) prove structural propositions (Prop. 3.1, 3.3) showing that if A_{\Gamma_\varphi} is 2-increasing, then \Gamma_\varphi must be piecewise constant/affine-on-\varphi(t)+t within each connected component where it lies below m_\varphi; (2) represent {t: \Gamma_\varphi<m_\varphi} as a countable union of disjoint open intervals and derive the explicit form on each interval with a unique junction point u_i^* solving \varphi(u_i^*)+u_i^*=m_\varphi(a_i)+\max\{b_i,\varphi(b_i)\}; (3) prove sufficiency by partitioning any rectangle into three types (above the curve, below the curve, and with two vertices on the curve) and verifying V(R)\ge 0 case-by-case using monotonicity of the max-terms and the compatibility condition.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: No empirical experiments, datasets, or numerical benchmarks are used. Validation is by formal proofs. Correctness is established via: (i) known properties of copulas/quasi-copulas (boundary conditions, Lipschitz/increasingness), (ii) explicit extremal formulas for B_{\Gamma_\varphi} and A_{\Gamma_\varphi}, and (iii) checking 2-increasingness through rectangle volumes V(R) with a proof strategy that reduces the general case to finitely many geometric rectangle configurations relative to the curve v=\varphi(u).
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Results are limited to the bivariate case and to curvilinear sections defined by \varphi in \Phi (continuous, strictly increasing bijections of [0,1] with fixed endpoints). The characterization applies specifically to the particular natural upper bound A_{\Gamma_\varphi} (the greatest quasi-copula with the given curvilinear section), not to the true pointwise supremum over all copulas with that section unless equality holds. The compatibility condition, while explicit, is global and may be nontrivial to verify or construct for complex \varphi and interval families. The work is theoretical and does not provide computational algorithms, numerical examples, or statistical/financial applications demonstrating impact on modeling.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Characterize when the supremum C_{\Gamma_\varphi}(u,v)=\sup\{C(u,v): C \text{ copula with curvilinear section }\Gamma_\varphi\} is itself a copula (noted as open even in the diagonal case). Develop constructive/algorithmic procedures to test compatibility and to build admissible interval families for a given \varphi and \Gamma_\varphi. Extend the theory to other sections (e.g., multiple curves, opposite/anti-diagonal-type curves) or to higher-dimensional copulas with prescribed sections. Investigate implications for dependence measures (tail dependence/asymmetry) tied to curvilinear sections and provide applied examples in finance or risk management.

Using small noise limit approach, we study degenerate stoch astic ergodic control problems and as a byproduct obtain error bou nds for the ε- optimal controls. We also establish tunneling for a special ergodic control problem and give a representation of the ergodic value using the tunneled Markov chain. 1. Introduction We study degenerate stochastic control problems using ”small no ise” perturba- tion analysis. i.e., we approach the original as a limit of non-degenerat e controlled diﬀusions given by small noise perturbations. This is in the spirit of a pr oposal of Kolmogorov as cited in [ 7] to select a ’physical solution’ for an ill-posed prob- lem by looking at the small noise limit of its stochastic perturbation. Th is is also the philosophy behind the vanishing viscosity method for solving elliptic /parabolic pdes. Since we are concerned with ergodic control problems, the b ehaviour of the invariant probability measures of the state dynamics enter the pict ure. Naturally one expects that the asymptotic behaviour of the invariant measu re of the small noise perturbation, as perturbation noise approach zero, play a r ole in the small noise limit of the ergodic control problem. Small noise perturbation o f dynamical systems governed by odes and the asymptotics of the invariant pr obability mea- sures is studied in Chapter 6, [ 9] when state space is compact and in [ 2] when state space is Rd. Small noise limit analysis leads to a selection procedure of invariant measure for the limiting dynamics which may possess multiple invariant p robability measures, see [ 15]. Analogous to the selection procedure for the invariant measures , does small noise perturbation of the ergodic optimal control prob lem selects in the limit a unique optimal ergodic control problem for the original degene rate controlled state dynamics We get an aﬃrmative answer under suitable condition s. We call this as ’physical’ ergodic control problem. The selection is achieved t hrough the selection of an invariant probability measure from the multiple invarian t probability measures of the optimal state dynamics and hence our result also c an be thought as a controlled version of the selection procedure described in [ 9]. For a special case, we see a tunneling of the optimal state dynamics and arrive at a repr esentation of the ergodic value through the tunneled Markov chain. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Studies degenerate (possibly non-elliptic) stochastic ergodic control via small-noise (vanishing viscosity) perturbations; proves a selection principle showing the ε→0 limit of optimal costs for suitably nondegenerate perturbations selects the “physical” ergodic value ρ* defined by minimization over all admissible stationary solution pairs/occupation measures (Def. 1.1(ii), ρ* = inf over ergodic occupation measures). Shows this selected value need not correspond to an optimal control uniformly for all initial states (Def. 1.1(i)), characterizing when optimality holds only on supports of selected invariant measures (Thm. 2.3–2.4). Provides sufficient conditions under which small-noise optimal controls converge to true optimal controls in the stronger sense (i), including asymptotically flat diffusions (K<0) with explicit O(√ε) error bounds (Thm. 3.3) and broader conditions ensuring convergence among stationary Markov controls (Thm. 4.6–4.9, 4.12). Establishes tunneling/metastability for 1D controlled gradient flows under optimal controls and represents the limiting ergodic value using a tunneled continuous-time Markov chain over deep wells (Thm. 5.10).
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Formulates ergodic control in relaxed-control/occupation-measure framework (controls valued in P(U)); uses tightness/weak convergence of stationary controlled diffusions and their ergodic occupation measures under small nondegenerate perturbations σ→σ_ε with σ_εσ_ε^T≥εI. Proves selection by identifying subsequential limits of optimal occupation measures and relating them to minimizers of the degenerate linear program over G. Develops coupling/comparison and Lyapunov-function stability arguments (inf-compact drift condition) to control invariant measures and empirical measures. In asymptotically flat case (K<0), derives quantitative bounds via Itô estimates on the difference X^ε−X and Lipschitz costs. For the beyond-flat case, introduces auxiliary bounding SDEs Y_i^ε driven by stabilizing drifts b_i and uses multidimensional comparison theorems plus uniform control of empirical measures (assumption D) to pass limits for stationary Markov controls, yielding ε-optimal computable controls via smoothing (convolution) of minimizing selectors. For constant diffusion, uses large deviations/quasi-potential estimates for invariant densities to obtain explicit exponentially small terms and conclude ρ*_U=ρ*_{USM}. For tunneling, applies Freidlin–Wentzell small-noise metastability: identifies wells, rescales time by e^{2λ/ε^2}, constructs the trace process on neighborhoods of minima, proves convergence to a CTMC with rates from local curvatures, and expresses ρ* as the stationary average cost over this chain.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: No empirical experiments or datasets. Validation is theoretical: (i) assumptions (A1),(L),(H1)/(H2) give selection theorem (Thm. 2.1) proved via tightness of optimal stationary pairs and weak limits of occupation measures; (ii) counterexample-style structural result (Thm. 2.4) shows lack of global optimality outside selected domains D0; (iii) asymptotically flat regime (K<0) gives explicit performance-gap bounds for optimal ε-controls versus true optimal (Thm. 3.3) using Itô/Gronwall; (iv) broader regime uses constructed perturbations σ_ε, comparison SDEs, Lyapunov drift inequalities, and condition (D) (with checkable sufficient condition Lem. 4.8) to prove convergence and ε-optimal stationary Markov controls (Thm. 4.6–4.9); (v) constant-diffusion specialization uses quasi-potential large deviations (Lemma 4.11) to derive explicit error bounds (Thm. 4.12); (vi) 1D gradient-flow example proves tunneling and Markov-chain representation (Thm. 5.7, 5.10).
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Results rely on nontrivial technical assumptions: stability/inf-compact Lyapunov conditions (L) and additional selection hypotheses (H1) or approximation hypothesis (H2) about convergence of invariant measures under perturbations, which may be hard to verify in general. In the general degenerate case, the small-noise limit selects the value for Def. 1.1(ii) and may fail to produce a control optimal for all initial states (Def. 1.1(i)); optimality may hold only on supports of selected invariant measures (domain D0), and outside D0 costs can be strictly larger (Thm. 2.4). Beyond asymptotic flatness, convergence is proved mainly within stationary Markov controls and requires assumption (D) controlling empirical measures of comparison processes; equality between ρ*_U and ρ*_{USM} is unresolved in general (addressed only in special cases like constant diffusion). Some key constructions assume smooth or continuous controls (e.g., smoothing by convolution, Usmooth_{SM}) and/or bounded costs in parts of Section 4. Tunneling/Markov-chain representation is restricted to 1D controlled gradient flows with additive control and several structural regularity/finite-critical-point assumptions (T), plus limits taken in a specific order (ε→0 then δ→0).
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: (1) Develop verifiable, general criteria replacing (H1)/(H2) for invariant-measure selection under controlled degenerate dynamics, possibly via PDE/viscosity or controllability/hypoellipticity conditions. (2) Characterize when the selected “physical” value ρ* coincides with the global optimal-control value in Def. 1.1(i) for all initial states, and quantify the structure/size of D0 in multidimensions. (3) Extend beyond stationary Markov controls: prove (or disprove) that ρ*_U=ρ*_{USM} under broader assumptions, and analyze existence/uniqueness of optimal selectors for degenerate HJB equations. (4) Provide computable schemes: numerical methods exploiting small-noise nondegenerate HJB/PDEs with rigorous error bounds for ε-optimal controls in higher dimensions, including adaptive ε selection. (5) Generalize tunneling analysis to multidimensional metastable controlled systems (non-gradient or controlled diffusions with multiple attractors), deriving effective Markov chains/rate matrices under optimal control and linking them to ergodic costs. (6) Study robustness to non-Feller/non-unique weak solutions and explore selection under different perturbation structures (state-dependent anisotropic noise, Lévy noise).

research_study_list.full_text: Multi-scale Cross-restoration Framework for Electrocardiogram Anomaly Detection Aofan Jiang1,2⋆, Chaoqin Huang1,2,4⋆, Qing Cao3, Shuang Wu3, Zi Zeng3, Kang Chen3, Ya Zhang1,2, and Yanfeng Wang1,2(� ) 1 Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2 Shanghai AI Laboratory 3 Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine 4 National University of Singapore {stillunnamed, huangchaoqin, shuang-renata, zengzidoct, ya_zhang, wangyanfeng}@sjtu.edu.cn, {cq30553, ck11208}@rjh.com.cn Abstract. Electrocardiogram(ECG)isawidelyuseddiagnostictoolfor detecting heart conditions. Rare cardiac diseases may be underdiagnosed using traditional ECG analysis, considering that no training dataset can exhaustallpossiblecardiacdisorders.Thispaperproposesusinganomaly detection to identify any unhealthy status, with normal ECGs solely for training. However, detecting anomalies in ECG can be challenging due to significant inter-individual differences and anomalies present in both global rhythm and local morphology. To address this challenge, this pa- per introduces a novel multi-scale cross-restoration framework for ECG anomaly detection and localization that considers both local and global ECG characteristics. The proposed framework employs a two-branch au- toencoder to facilitate multi-scale feature learning through a masking and restoration process, with one branch focusing on global features from the entire ECG and the other on local features from heartbeat- level details, mimicking the diagnostic process of cardiologists. Anoma- lies are identified by their high restoration errors. To evaluate the per- formance on a large number of individuals, this paper introduces a new challenging benchmark with signal point-level ground truths annotated by experienced cardiologists. The proposed method demonstrates state- of-the-art performance on this benchmark and two other well-known ECG datasets. The benchmark dataset and source code are available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/ECGAD Keywords: Anomaly Detection· Electrocardiogram 1 Introduction The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a monitoring tool widely used to evaluate the heart status of patients and provide information on cardiac electrophysiology. Developing automated analysis systems capable of detecting and identifying ab- normal signals is crucial in light of the importance of ECGs in medical diagnosis ⋆ Equal contribution arXiv:2308.01639v1  [cs.CV]  3 Aug 20232 A. Jiang et al. and the need to ease the workload of clinicians. However, training a classifier on labeled ECGs that focus on specific diseases may not recognize new abnormal statuses that were not encountered during training, given the diversity and rar- ity of cardiac diseases [8,16,23]. On the other hand, anomaly detection, which is trained only on normal healthy data, can identify any potential abnormal status and avoid the failure to detect rare cardiac diseases [10,17,21]. The current anomaly detection techniques, including one-class discriminative approaches [2,14], reconstruction-based approaches [15,30], and self-supervised learning-based approaches [3,26], all operate under the assumption that models trained solely on normal data will struggle to process anomalous data and thus the substantial drop in performance presents an indication of anomalies. While anomaly detection has been widely used in the medical field to analyze medical images [12,24] and time-series data [18,29], detecting anomalies in ECG data is particularly challenging due to the substantial inter-individual differences and the presence of anomalies in both global rhythm and local morphology. So far, few studies have investigated anomaly detection in ECG [11,29]. TSL [29] uses expert knowledge-guided amplitude- and frequency-based data transformations to simulate anomalies for different individuals. BeatGAN [11] employs a genera- tive adversarial network to separately reconstruct normalized heartbeats instead of the entire raw ECG signal. While BeatGAN alleviates individual differences, it neglects the important global rhythm information of the ECG. This paper proposes a novel multi-scale cross-restoration framework for ECG anomaly detection and localization. To our best knowledge, this is the first work to integrate both local and global characteristics for ECG anomaly detection. To take into account multi-scale data, the framework adopts a two-branch autoen- coder architecture, with one branch focusing on global features from the entire ECG and the other on local features from heartbeat-level details. A multi-scale cross-attention module is introduced, which learns to combine the two feature types for making the final prediction. This module imitates the diagnostic pro- cess followed by experienced cardiologists who carefully examine both the en- tire ECG and individual heartbeats to detect abnormalities in both the overall rhythm and the specific local morphology of the signal [7]. Each of the branches employs a masking and restoration strategy,i.e., the model learns how to per- form temporal-dependent signal inpainting from the adjacent unmasked regions within a specific individual. Such context-aware restoration has the advantage of making the restoration less susceptible to individual differences. During testing, anomalies are identified as samples or regions with high restoration errors. To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed method on a large number of individuals, we adopt the public PTB-XL database [22] with only patient-level diagnoses, and ask experienced cardiologists to provide signal point-level localization annotations. The resulting dataset is then introduced as a large-scale challenging benchmark for ECG anomaly detection and localization. The proposed method is evaluated on this challenging benchmark as well as on two traditional ECG anomaly detection benchmarks [6,13]. The experimental re- sults have shown that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-artMulti-scale Cross-restoration Framework for ECG Anomaly Detection 3 TGM Random MaskM! Formally, given a set ofN nor- mal ECGs denoted as{xi, i= 1, ..., N}, wherexi ∈ RD represents the vectorized representation of thei-th ECG consisting ofD signal points, the objective is to trainacomputationalmodelcapableofidentifyingwhetheranewECGisnormal or anomalous, and localize the regions of anomalies in abnormal ECGs. 2.1 Multi-scale Cross-restoration In Fig. 1, we present an overview of our two-branch framework for ECG anomaly detection. One branch is responsible for learning global ECG features, while the other focuses on local heartbeat details. Our framework comprises four main components: (i) masking and encoding, (ii) multi-scale cross-attention module, (iii)uncertainty-awarerestoration,and(iv)trendgenerationmodule.Weprovide detailed explanations of each of these components in the following sections. Masking and Encoding.Given a pair consisting of a global ECG signalxg ∈ RD and a randomly selected local heartbeatxl ∈ Rd segmented from xg for training, as shown in Fig. 1, we apply two random masks,Mg and Ml, to mask xg and xl, respectively. To enable multi-scale feature learning,Ml is applied to a consecutive small region to facilitate detail restoration, whileMg is applied to several distinct regions distributed throughout the whole sequence to facilitate global rhythm restoration. The masked signals are processed separately by global4 A. Jiang et al. and local encoders,Eg and El, resulting in global featurefin g = Eg(xg ⊙ Mg) and local featurefin l = El(xl ⊙Ml), where⊙ denotes the element-wise product. Multi-scale Cross-attention.To capture the relationship between global and local features, we use the self-attention mechanism [20] on the concatenated feature of fin g and fin l . Specifically, the attention mechanism is expressed as Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKT √dk )V , whereQ, K, Vare identical input terms, while √dk is the square root of the feature dimension used as a scaling fac- tor. Self-attention is achieved by settingQ = K = V = concat(fin g , fin l ). The cross-attention feature,fca, is obtained from the self-attention mechanism, which dynamically weighs the importance of each element in the combined feature. To obtain the final outputs of the global and local features, fout g and fout l , containing cross-scale information, we consider residual connections: fout g = fin g +ϕg(fca), fout l = fin l +ϕl(fca), whereϕg(·) and ϕl(·) are MLP architectures with two fully connected layers. Uncertainty-aware Restoration. Targeting signal restorations, features of fout g and fout l are decoded by two decoders, Dg and Dl, to obtain restored signals ˆxg and ˆxl, respectively, along with corresponding restoration uncertainty maps σg and σl measuring the difficulty of restoration for various signal points, where ˆxg, σg = Dg(fout g ), ˆxl, σl = Dl(fout l ). An uncertainty-aware restoration loss is used to incorporate restoration uncertainty into the loss functions, Lglobal = DX k=1 {(xk g − ˆxk g)2 σkg + logσk g }, Llocal = dX k=1 {(xk l − ˆxk l )2 σk l + logσk l }, (1) where for each function, the first term is normalized by the corresponding un- certainty, and the second term prevents predicting a large uncertainty for all restoration pixels following [12]. The superscriptk represents the position of the k-th element of the signal. It is worth noting that, unlike [12], the uncertainty- aware loss is used for restoration, but not for reconstruction. Trend Generation Module.The trend generation module (TGM) illustrated in Fig. 1 generates a smooth time-series trend xt ∈ RD by removing signal details, which is represented as the smooth difference between adjacent time- series signal points. An autoencoder (Et and Dt) encodes the trend information into Et(xt), which are concatenated with the global featurefout g to restore the global ECGˆxt = Dt(concat(Et(xt), fout g )). The restoration loss is defined as the Euclidean distance betweenxg and ˆxt, Ltrend = PD k=1(xk g − ˆxk t )2. This process guides global feature learning using time-series trend information, emphasizing rhythm characteristics while de-emphasizing morphological details. Loss Function.The final loss function for optimizing our model during the training process can be written as L = Lglobal + αLlocal + βLtrend, (2) where α and β are trade-off parameters weighting the loss function. For simplic- ity, we adoptα = β = 1.0 as the default.Multi-scale Cross-restoration Framework for ECG Anomaly Detection 5 2.2 Anomaly Score Measurement For each test samplex, local ECGs from the segmented heartbeat set{xl,m, m= 1, ..., M} arepairedwiththeglobalECG xg oneatatimeasinputs.Theanomaly score A(x) is calculated to estimate the abnormality, A(x) = DX k=1 (xk g − ˆxk g)2 σkg + MX m=1 dX k=1 (xk l,m − ˆxk l,m)2 σk l,m + DX k=1 (xk g − ˆxk t )2, (3) where the three terms correspond to global restoration, local restoration, and trend restoration, respectively. For localization, an anomaly score map is gener- ated in the same way as Eq. (3), but without summing over the signal points. The anomalies are indicated by relatively large anomaly scores, and vice versa. 3 Experiments Datasets Three publicly available ECG datasets are used to evaluate the pro- posed method, including PTB-XL [22], MIT-BIH [13], and Keogh ECG [6]. – PTB-XL database includes clinical 12-lead ECGs that are 10 seconds in length for each patient, with only patient-levelannotations. To build a new challenging anomaly detection and localizationbenchmark, 8167 normal ECGs are used for training, while 912 normal and 1248 abnormal ECGs are used for testing. We provide signal point-levelannotations of 400 ECGs, including 22 different abnormal types, that were annotated by two experi- enced cardiologists. To our best knowledge, we are the first to explore ECG anomaly detection and localization across various patients on such a complex and large-scale database. – MIT-BIHarrhythmia dataset divides the ECGs from 44 patients into inde- pendent heartbeats based on the annotated R-peak position, following [11]. 62436 normal heartbeats are used for training, while 17343 normal and 9764 abnormal beats are used for testing, with heartbeat-levelannotations. – Keogh ECGdataset includes 7 ECGs from independent patients, evaluat- ing anomaly localization with signal point-levelannotations. For each ECG, there is an anomaly subsequence that corresponds to a pre-ventricular con- traction, while the remaining sequence is used as normal data to train the model. The ECGs are partitioned into fixed-length sequences of 320 by a sliding window with a stride of 40 during training and 160 during testing. Evaluation ProtocolsThe performance of anomaly detection and localization is quantified using the area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC), with a higher AUC value indicating a better method. To ensure compa- rability across different annotation levels, we used patient-level, heartbeat-level, and signal point-level AUC for each respective setting. For heartbeat-level clas- sification, the F1 score is also reported following [11]. For a fair comparison, we re-trained all the methods under the same experimental setup. Anomaly DetectionThe anomaly detection performance on PTB-XL is sum- marized in Table 1. The proposed method achieves 86.0% AUC in patient-level anomaly detection and outperforms all baselines by a large margin (10.3%). Ta- ble 2 displays the comparison results on MIT-BIH, where the proposed method achieves a heartbeat-level AUC of 96.9%, showing an improvement of 2.4% over the state-of-the-art BeatGAN (94.5%). Furthermore, the F1-score of the pro- posed method is 88.3%, which is 6.7% higher than BeatGAN (81.6%). Table 4 shows that each module contributes positively to the overall performance of the framework. When none of the modules were employed, the method becomes a ECG reconstruction ap- proach with a naive L2 loss and lacks cross-attention in multi-scale data. When individually adding the MR, MC, UL, and TGM modules to the baseline model without any of them, the AUC values improve from 70.4% to 80.4%, 80.3%, 72.8%, and 71.2%, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of each module. Moreover, as the modules are added in sequence, the performance improves step by step from 70.4% to 86.0% in AUC, highlighting the combined impact of all modules on the proposed framework. We conduct a sensitivity analysis on the mask ratio, as shown in Table 5. Restoration with a 0% masking ratio can be regarded as reconstruction, which takes an entire sample as input and its target is to output the input sample. Results indicate that the model’s performance first improves and then declines as the mask ratio increases from 0% to 70%. This trend is due to the fact that a low mask ratio can limit the model’s feature learning ability during restoration,Multi-scale Cross-restoration Framework for ECG Anomaly Detection 9 while a high ratio can make it increasingly difficult to restore the masked regions. Therefore, there is a trade-off between maximizing the model’s potential and ensuringareasonablerestorationdifficulty.Theoptimalmaskratiois30%,which achieves the highest anomaly detection result (86.0% in AUC). 4 Conclusion This paper proposes a novel framework for ECG anomaly detection, where fea- tures of the entire ECG and local heartbeats are combined with a masking- restoration process to detect anomalies, simulating the diagnostic process of cardiologists. A challenging benchmark, with signal point-level annotations pro- vided by experienced cardiologists, is proposed, facilitating future research in ECG anomaly localization. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its potential in real-world clinical diagnosis. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: Proposes an unsupervised ECG anomaly detection and localization approach trained only on normal ECGs that explicitly combines global rhythm and local morphology information. Introduces a multi-scale cross-restoration framework with (i) two-branch global- and heartbeat-level autoencoders, (ii) cross-attention to fuse scales, (iii) masking-based context-aware restoration to mitigate inter-individual variation, (iv) uncertainty-aware restoration losses, and (v) a trend generation module to emphasize rhythm. Releases a new challenging PTB-XL-based benchmark with cardiologist-provided signal point-level localization annotations; demonstrates state-of-the-art detection and localization on PTB-XL, MIT-BIH, and Keogh ECG.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: Two-branch convolutional autoencoder pipeline. For training, pair a full ECG x_g with a randomly selected heartbeat x_l segmented via R-peak detection. Apply different random masks: global mask over multiple dispersed regions (rhythm) and local mask over one contiguous region (morphology). Encode masked inputs with E_g and E_l, concatenate features and pass through self-attention to obtain cross-attention feature f_ca; add residual MLP projections to yield cross-scale features f_out^g and f_out^l. Decode to restored signals \hat{x}_g, \hat{x}_l and per-timepoint uncertainty maps \sigma_g, \sigma_l; optimize an uncertainty-weighted restoration loss sum_k ( (x-\hat{x})^2/\sigma + log \sigma ). Add a Trend Generation Module that extracts a smoothed trend x_t, encodes it, concatenates with global features, and restores \hat{x}_t with L2 loss to enforce rhythm-focused representation. At test time, compute anomaly score as the sum of global, local (over all beats), and trend restoration errors (uncertainty-weighted), and obtain a pointwise anomaly map for localization.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Datasets: (1) PTB-XL 12-lead, 10s ECGs. Train: 8167 normal ECGs. Test: 912 normal + 1248 abnormal. For localization, 400 ECGs annotated at signal point level by two experienced cardiologists spanning 22 abnormal types. Metrics: patient-level AUC for detection; signal point-level AUC for localization. (2) MIT-BIH Arrhythmia: heartbeat-segmented via provided R-peaks; train 62,436 normal beats; test 17,343 normal + 9,764 abnormal; metrics heartbeat-level AUC and F1. (3) Keogh ECG: 7 single-patient sequences with point-level anomaly subsequences; train on normal parts; window length 320, stride 40 (train) / 160 (test); metric point-level AUC per patient and average. Preprocessing: Butterworth + notch filtering; R-peak detection with adaptive threshold; heartbeat segmentation. Training: convolutional AE backbone (as in BeatGAN), AdamW lr 1e-4, weight decay 1e-5, 50 epochs, batch 32, cosine LR schedule; default loss weights α=β=1.0. Baselines re-trained under same setup; ablations on PTB-XL for masking/restoration, cross-attention, uncertainty loss, and trend module; mask-ratio sensitivity (0–70%, best at 30%).
llm_extracted_info.limitations: Relies on accurate preprocessing and R-peak detection/heartbeat segmentation; errors there may degrade the local branch. Assumes sufficient normal-only coverage; unusual but healthy variants or distribution shift across devices/leads/populations could raise false positives. Restoration-error methods can be sensitive to abrupt changes and may produce narrower anomaly regions than clinician annotations; localization quality depends on thresholding/interpretation. Computationally heavier than single-branch models because it evaluates multiple beats per ECG at test time; reported inference is ~4.2 fps with ~2.4 GB GPU memory. Uses fixed hyperparameters (e.g., mask ratio, α=β=1) and a CNN AE backbone; may not be optimal for all datasets. Benchmark localization labels are provided for only a subset (400) of PTB-XL test ECGs and were annotated by two cardiologists, leaving potential inter-rater variability.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Extend to multi-lead-aware modeling (explicit inter-lead attention/graph structure) and evaluate robustness across acquisition devices and sampling rates. Reduce test-time cost via beat aggregation, learned beat selection, or a single-pass model producing global+local scores. Explore stronger self-supervised pretraining or diffusion/transformer backbones while preserving patient-specific invariances. Improve calibration and interpretability of uncertainty maps and link localized anomalies to clinically meaningful waveform components (P/QRS/T) and diagnoses. Expand the benchmark with more point-level annotations, multi-rater agreement studies, and semi-supervised settings that incorporate limited abnormal labels. Investigate domain adaptation and continual learning to handle population shift and rare/novel arrhythmias without catastrophic forgetting.
